questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the character a foil is defined against.
questions.stem: During a night handover, Ilda's neighbour Marek is quiet and methodical while she acts on impulse. What is Marek for?

options.text: Marek is a plot convenience who exists only to move the action elsewhere
options.misconception: believes a foil exists only to move the plot along

options.text: Marek is Ilda's double because both women share the same nursing training
options.misconception: confuses shared background with the contrast a foil requires

options.text: Marek is Ilda's foil, defined by contrasting with her impulsiveness
Marek is a minor figure whose only purpose is to be mentioned once
options.misconception: assumes a foil must be unimportant to count as one

questions.explanation: A foil is defined by contrast, so Marek's steadiness throws Ilda's impulsiveness into relief. Shared training, plot convenience and one-line mentions do not establish a foil.
questions.hint: Ask what Marek's qualities make visible in Ilda.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a subplot changes the pressure on the main action.
questions.stem: A handover notes that while the ward traced who had been signing off the wrong doses, a quieter story about a borrowed radio ran underneath. How does that subplot work?

answer.exemplar: The borrowed-radio subplot works as a counter-pressure: it keeps a supply of ordinary care visible while the main action is consumed by the investigation, and it eventually supplies the colleague who confirms the forged signatures. It therefore does double duty, deepening the world and creating the turn that the main plot needs.

questions.explanation: A subplot earns its place by pressing on the main action rather than running beside it. Here the radio thread supplies both ordinary texture and the witness the investigation needs.
questions.hint: Consider what the radio thread contributes.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A subplot's function in a novel
questions.learningObjective: Defend a subplot by the pressure it puts on the main plot.
questions.stem: In a handover, a junior nurse defends the ward novel by insisting the kitchen scenes have no effect on the crisis. What is the strongest rebuttal?

options.text: The kitchen scenes slow the plot, so the criticism about pacing is fair
options.misconception: accepts that pace complaints are the only test of a subplot

options.text: The scenes shape the crisis by making the ward's habits visible before it breaks
Nothing is lost by skipping them, since the crisis resolves without them
options.misconception: believes a subplot must change outcomes to matter at all

options.text: The scenes matter only because they describe the hospital's older traditions
options.misconception: reduces a subplot's value to background detail

questions.explanation: A subplot functions when it shapes the main action, often by exposing habits that later matter. The junior's defence fails because it tests the scenes only against outcomes, not against function.
questions.hint: Focus on how the crisis grows out of what the scenes show.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the effect of a change in how a case is reported.

stimulus.body: Night sister notes that the handover itself has changed. What the ward once passed on in person is now read from a printed sheet, and the juniors are told not to question the numbers. She asks the registrar to say plainly who now holds the story of a patient.

questions.stem: According to the handover note, what has the change in how information is passed mainly produced?

options.text: A narrower and less reliable account, because the juniors are told not to question it
A single reliable account of the ward, since printed sheets cannot be argued with
options.misconception: believes written handover removes the chance of distortion

options.text: The same reliability the ward always had, because the numbers stay unchanged
options.misconception: assumes the facts stay fixed even when the telling changes

options.text: No change at all, since a handover is only ever an administrative routine
options.misconception: dismisses a handover as mere administration

questions.explanation: When a shift's account narrows to an unchallengeable sheet, reliability drops rather than rises. The note's detail about juniors not questioning points at a restricted point of view.
questions.hint: Focus on who may question the account and who may not.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A viewpoint shift that supplies a reason
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a change of speaker creates doubt.
questions.stem: A handover records a case where the story of an accident was told first by the sister on nights and then by the day porter, and the version the patient later repeated matched neither. Why does the handover treat the switch of speaker as important?

options.text: The change matters because each speaker was paid to describe events in their own way
options.misconception: reads the switch as a matter of wages and habit

options.text: The change matters because hospital policy requires two accounts of any accident
options.misconception: invents a policy rule to explain a formal handover

options.text: The change matters because the patient could not remember which speaker had come
options.misconception: blames the patient's memory instead of the narration

options.text: The change matters because the second speaker supplies a reason to doubt the first

questions.explanation: Moving the account to a second speaker is a device: it introduces doubt about the first account and offers a reason for the change in what we believe. Policy and pay are beside the point.
questions.hint: Ask what the second account does to belief in the first.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the narrator of a handover account.
questions.stem: At handover the ward sister describes a patient who has been told twice that his hearing is fine, and she adds that she checked with the community nurse. Who is the narrator here?

options.text: The ward sister, because the report is given in her own voice and standards
The reader, because the details arrive without any source being named
options.misconception: confuses an unnamed source with an absent narrator

options.text: The patient, because the phrase about his hearing comes from his own report
options.misconception: assumes a quoted line makes that character the narrator

options.text: The day team, because handover notes belong to whoever reads them next
options.misconception: treats the readership of a report as its speaker

questions.explanation: The handover is voiced throughout by the sister, including her own checking habit, so she is the narrator. An unnamed source is still a source, and a reader is not a speaker.
questions.hint: Ask whose voice and habits the handover speaks in.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Weigh contradictory entries to test a speaker's reliability.
questions.stem: One entry in the handover insists the patient has been walking unaided since Tuesday, while an earlier entry says a frame was ordered for the stairs. How should the later claim be read?

answer.exemplar: The later claim should be read as an overstatement by the teller rather than a settled fact. It sits alongside an entry that records a frame being ordered, so a careful reader holds both and treats the confident walking claim as the speaker's wishful version, not as evidence that the frame was never needed.

questions.explanation: Two entries that contradict each other mark the later one as an overstatement. The reader must weigh both rather than accept the confident version.
questions.hint: Weigh the two entries against each other.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Analyse how a foil measures another character.
questions.stem: A handover reports a reader who said the night porter, who speaks only about the heating, counts as a foil to the ward sister. Which answer holds up?

options.text: Because he is the only character who mentions the heating at all
options.misconception: mistakes unique mention for the contrast a foil requires

options.text: Because his narrow concern with heating shows how narrow her own world has become
Because his presence keeps the ward from feeling empty during the night
options.misconception: treats a foil's purpose as filling out the setting

options.text: Because the ward sister never manages to speak when he is in the room
options.misconception: reads a foil as a device for silencing another character

questions.explanation: A foil works by contrast of scale and concern, so the porter's narrowness measures the sister's own narrowing. Mere presence, unique mention and silencing do not make him a foil.
questions.hint: Ask what the porter's narrowness shows about the sister.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the function of a subplot from a witness's account.

stimulus.body: The registrar asks whether the story of the two students who share a flat near the hospital matters at all, since no patient is named in it. The sister replies that the flat is where the borrowed temperature charts were first hidden.

questions.stem: On this handover's reasoning, what function does the students' flat serve in the story?

options.text: It serves to give the ward a little ordinary life away from the wards
options.misconception: reduces the subplot to background texture alone

options.text: It serves to show how the students spend their evenings after a shift
options.misconception: reads the subplot as a study of student leisure

options.text: It serves the main plot by hiding the borrowed charts that prove the tampering
It serves to establish how far the hospital is from the students' homes
options.misconception: mistakes a geographical detail for the subplot's function

questions.explanation: The sister's reply makes the flat a mechanism: the hiding place for the borrowed charts is what the investigation turns on. Ordinary texture and location would not make the thread necessary.
questions.hint: Listen to how the sister answers the registrar's question.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A subplot's function in a novel
questions.learningObjective: Compare two novels to isolate what makes a subplot work.
questions.stem: A handover compares two novels in which a gardener's illness runs alongside a family's dispute, and asks what makes the first version work while the second leaves the thread slack.

options.text: The first works because the illness ends before the dispute is settled
options.misconception: credits timing rather than the thread's effect on the plot

options.text: The first works because the gardener appears in more than half the chapters
options.misconception: measures weight by how often a character appears

options.text: The first works because the dispute is harder to follow than the illness
options.misconception: judges a subplot by how confusing the main plot becomes

options.text: The first works because the illness changes what the family can settle

questions.explanation: A subplot functions when it constrains or redirects the main action, and the illness here decides what the family can resolve. Ending, frequency and confusion do not account for the difference.
questions.hint: Ask what the illness decides for the family.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Determine the effect of a shifted point of view.
questions.stem: In a handover, a family is told about the ward's decision to transfer a patient by hearing it from the patient herself, who repeats it in her own flat voice. What is the effect of that point-of-view shift?

options.text: It lets the reader weigh the family's reaction against the ward's account
It removes any doubt about the decision, because the patient was present
options.misconception: believes presence at an event guarantees accuracy

options.text: It shows the ward hiding the decision from the family on purpose
options.misconception: reads a shift in voice as deliberate concealment

options.text: It makes the decision unimportant, since it is only reported second-hand
options.misconception: confuses point of view with the weight of the news

questions.explanation: Moving the report into the patient's voice puts the ward's version and the family's response in one frame, letting the reader weigh them. It neither guarantees accuracy nor proves concealment.
questions.hint: Consider what the reader can now compare.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A viewpoint shift that supplies a reason
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a second account unsettles a first.
questions.stem: A handover notes that the account of the night fire was taken first from the porter who smelled smoke and later from the electrician who found the fault. Why does the second telling matter so much?

answer.exemplar: The second telling matters because it gives the reader a reason to doubt the first. The porter's account is sensory and certain, yet the electrician's evidence offers a cause the porter never saw, so the change of speaker supplies both a rival explanation and a motive for treating the earlier testimony as incomplete.

questions.explanation: A shift of speaker supplies a reason for doubt because the second account carries evidence the first never mentioned. Sensory certainty and unseen causes leave the reader holding two versions.
questions.hint: Ask what the electrician adds to the porter's account.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Judge how a handover's voice shapes trust in it.
questions.stem: A new sister writes her first handover as a list of facts about beds, doses and families, with no mention of who noticed the odd temperature. The registrar says she has made the shift sound like an inventory, and asks her what she wants the ward to do with what she wrote.

options.text: That a handover should contain more facts about the beds
options.misconception: reads the comment as a demand for more detail

options.text: That the new sister should write the handover in a warmer voice
options.misconception: treats the criticism as a matter of tone

options.text: That a flat factual voice can make the ward seem like an inventory
That inventories are unsuitable for handing over care at all
options.misconception: generalises from one note to condemn the handover form

questions.explanation: The registrar is pointing at how the note's flat voice makes the ward look like an inventory, which is a question of trust and effect. More facts or warmer wording would miss that.
questions.hint: Notice the word the registrar chooses for the new note.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Identify evidence that undercuts a confident account.

stimulus.body: A handover says the ward sister reported that a patient was completely fine, then added, almost as an afterthought, that the patient's daughter had not visited for nine days. The registrar asks what the note is doing by placing the second detail where it stands.

questions.stem: According to the handover, what is the note doing with that second detail?

options.text: It is offering two unrelated observations about the same patient
options.misconception: reads the remarks as unrelated rather than revealing

options.text: It is undercutting the confidence of the clinical summary from within
It is showing that the ward does not keep track of visiting relatives
options.misconception: redirects the note towards a procedural complaint

options.text: It is admitting that the ward's own record of visits is incomplete
options.misconception: reads the aside as an admission about the paperwork

questions.explanation: The aside about the daughter shows the reassuring summary is not the whole picture, casting doubt on the narrator from within. Reading the remarks as unrelated misses the design.
questions.hint: Ask why the detail about visits is placed last.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the foil function of a contrasted character.
questions.stem: In a handover the pharmacist is described as careful, unobtrusive and, in the sister's words, the opposite of how I work. Why does the handover treat the pharmacist as a foil?

options.text: The pharmacist serves to show the sister how she ought to work
options.misconception: reads a foil as a model of correct behaviour

options.text: The pharmacist serves to lend the ward some professional authority
options.misconception: mistakes a professional role for the contrasting function

options.text: The pharmacist serves to keep the sister's dispensing habits under watch
options.misconception: reframes a literary contrast as a supervision duty

options.text: The pharmacist serves as a foil that throws the sister's manner into relief

questions.explanation: The sister names the contrast herself, which is the definition of a foil: the pharmacist's manner highlights her own. A model to imitate, a badge of authority and a supervisor are different things.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Identify how a subplot feeds a main plot.
questions.stem: A handover describes a chart dispute between two doctors running beneath the ward's real business of a discharge that went wrong. What does the chart dispute contribute?

options.text: It establishes the habit of two versions of a file, which the discharge error repeats
It adds a second dispute so the ward's business looks busier
options.misconception: judges a thread by how much activity it adds

options.text: It shows the two doctors disagree about how patients should be treated
options.misconception: reduces the thread to a clinical disagreement

options.text: It gives the reader a reason to distrust the discharge decision on its own
options.misconception: mistakes a supplied pattern for a supplied verdict

questions.explanation: The subplot matters because the habit it establishes is the habit behind the main error, so it feeds the plot rather than decorating it. A second dispute and a verdict are other things.
questions.hint: Ask whether the habit repeats in the main plot.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A subplot's function in a novel
questions.learningObjective: Defend a thread by its pressure on the main plot.
questions.stem: A handover states that a critic who said the bakery thread in a war novel had nothing to do with the war was describing the thread, not judging it. Explain what the thread actually contributes.

answer.exemplar: The bakery thread contributes by acting on the war plot: its owner decides who can leave the town, and that decision controls the town's movements during the fighting. Because the thread supplies the means by which the war is fought and suffered, it is structural rather than decorative, and the critic's complaint about pace never addresses the question of what the thread does.

questions.explanation: A thread functions when it acts on the main plot, and here the bakery decides who may leave, which is the war's own business. Relief, background and mere quality do not explain why it is needed.
questions.hint: Ask what the bakery decides that matters to the war.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Analyse how a change in reporting reshapes a known place.
questions.stem: Under the old arrangement the sister described the ward to new nurses in words as she walked them round. The new arrangement sends a printed summary ahead of the visit, and she notices that newcomers now ask about the summary rather than about the people in the beds.

options.text: The change makes newcomers care about documentation more than about patients
options.misconception: redirects the effect from the account to the reader's taste

options.text: The change gives experienced staff a reason to shorten their walking rounds
options.misconception: reads a change in perspective as a change in workload

options.text: The change means the summary is a less accurate record than the old verbal account
options.misconception: assumes that a change of medium must reduce accuracy

options.text: The change means the ward is known first as a document and later as people

questions.explanation: The ward is known first as a document and later as people, so the viewpoint shifts from the living round to the summary prepared in advance. The other readings misread it as subject matter.
questions.hint: Ask what the ward becomes before the round begins.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a second account unsettles a first.

questions.stem: Why does the handover treat the passenger's account as doing real work?

options.text: It shows the driver is lying about the light, so the case is closed
options.misconception: treats the second account as proof of deliberate deceit

options.text: It gives the reader a reason to doubt the driver's certainty
It proves the light changed, so the driver cannot be blamed at all
options.misconception: converts one alternative account into a settled verdict

options.text: It shows that passengers remember traffic lights better than drivers
options.misconception: turns the device into a claim about memory in general

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Assess a narrator's reliance on unnamed sources.
questions.stem: A handover contains the sentence, The night was uneventful, as those who were there will confirm. Why does the handover treat that sentence as a claim about the speaker?

options.text: It shows the speaker knows exactly what happened on that shift
options.misconception: reads an appeal to others as a claim of complete knowledge

options.text: It shows the speaker is a neutral reporter with no stake in the ward's reputation
options.misconception: reads a formulaic assurance as proof of neutrality

options.text: It shows the speaker relies on unnamed others to certify what cannot be checked
It shows the speaker is deliberately accusing the night staff of hiding things
options.misconception: turns a vague phrase into a specific accusation

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Weigh a general claim against a dated record.
questions.stem: One handover line says a patient was completely compliant, and the same file describes repeated refusals of the evening dose. How should a reader hold both?

options.text: The specific record entries should outweigh the general summary as evidence
The two statements cancel out, so nothing can be concluded about the patient
options.misconception: treats a contradiction as the end of any inquiry

options.text: The general summary should be preferred, since it reflects the overall impression
options.misconception: prefers impression to documented particulars

options.text: The later entries should be preferred, since they were written with better information
options.misconception: assumes a later entry is automatically better informed

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a foil works through contrast of scale.
questions.stem: A handover defends a character who is dull on purpose, so that the ward seems sensible by contrast. Explain what that defence assumes about how a foil works.

answer.exemplar: The defence assumes that contrast is a legitimate literary purpose, which is exactly what makes a foil a foil: a character defined by a quality set against the quality of another character. Dullness here is not a failure of invention but a chosen position, and it does the ward's character the service of making the reader measure the ward against the dullness rather than against the writer's invention.

questions.explanation: The defence describes a foil accurately, since contrast is the role's purpose. Nothing requires the dull character to be silent, and the defence is not about literary merit in general.
questions.hint: Ask whether contrast counts as a deliberate purpose.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a subplot by its effect on what the ward knows.
questions.stem: The registrar notes that a new nurse keeps two notebooks, one for ward business and one for a patient she visits on her days off. The registrar asks whether the second notebook is doing any work for the ward's story or only serving her conscience.

options.text: It serves only the nurse's conscience and has no effect on the ward's story
options.misconception: dismisses a subplot that stays outside the ward's rooms

options.text: It shapes the ward's story because the visits eventually alter what the ward knows
It shows that good nurses keep records that colleagues would not keep
options.misconception: reads the subplot as a lesson about nursing standards

options.misconception: treats a subplot as a rival story rather than a pressure

questions.explanation: The registrar asks about work, and the honest answer is that the thread alters what the ward learns and can therefore affect the main action. Conscience and rivalry describe theme, not function.
questions.hint: Ask whether the visits change what the ward ends up knowing.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A subplot's function in a novel
questions.learningObjective: Explain why one thread holds a reader and another does not.

stimulus.body: A handover compares a romance thread in one novel with a thread about a shop in another, and asks why the second holds the reader while the first does not. The registrar notes that the shopkeeper in the second novel is also the only person who knows where the money is kept.

questions.stem: On the handover's reasoning, why does the shop thread hold the reader?

options.text: The shop is described with more sensory detail than the romance
options.misconception: credits description rather than structural effect

options.text: The romance ends earlier, so it has less time to affect the plot
options.misconception: treats length of a thread as its measure of force

options.text: The shopkeeper keeps the money that the main plot depends on
The romance is told from a point of view the reader finds less clear
options.misconception: blames a thread's narration for its structural weakness

questions.explanation: The shop holds the reader because its owner controls resources the main plot needs, so the thread is structurally indispensable. Detail, length and clarity of narration do not explain that.
questions.hint: Ask what the main plot needs from the thread.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Determine the effect of relaying information at one remove.
questions.stem: During a handover, the registrar describes a case where the ward's findings were relayed to the family by a nurse who had not met the patient. Why does the handover treat the relay as a point-of-view decision?

options.misconception: assumes relay always improves accuracy

options.text: It hides the ward's judgement behind the messenger's neutral words

options.misconception: turns a narrative choice into a procedural complaint

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Identify which observation would test a narrator's faithfulness.
questions.stem: A handover reports a speaker whose account of the ward is warm in every particular, and asks which observation would most weaken the claim that this is a faithful record.

answer.exemplar: The observation that would most weaken the claim is a checkable error inside the record, such as a wrong date for the day the new trolley arrived. Warmth of manner, volume of detail and popularity among colleagues are impressions, and impressions cannot be checked against the ward's own papers, whereas a single misstated date can be tested.

questions.explanation: A checkable error inside the record is what tests faithfulness, since warmth of manner proves nothing about accuracy. Detail, reputation and vocabulary are impressions rather than evidence.
questions.hint: Ask which observation could be checked against a record.

questions.stem: A patient's own account says the lights were off all night, but the file records a lamp being moved at two in the morning and the night sister who admits she was awake. The handover asks the registrar to say who is telling the story of that night and how much of it can be trusted.

options.text: The patient's, because a person in bed cannot be expected to observe the ward
options.misconception: judges a claim by the observer's position, not the evidence

options.text: The night sister's, because admitting to being awake proves she invented it
options.misconception: treats one admitted detail as disproof of the whole account

options.text: Neither, because the file and the sister support exactly the same thing
options.misconception: reads corroborating details as proof both accounts are sound

options.text: The patient's, because the file and the sister both point to the lamp

questions.explanation: Two independent details, the moved lamp and the sister's admission, both contradict the patient's certainty, so that account is the one that fails. The confession supports her telling.
questions.hint: Weigh the two details that contradict the patient.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the foil function of a contrasted character.

stimulus.body: A handover mentions a ward's night porter, who says little and is entirely occupied with the heating, and the ward sister, whose evenings are given to complaints and unfinished paperwork. A member of staff remarks that the porter seems to come from a different ward altogether.

questions.stem: According to the handover, the porter's function is most accurately described as

options.text: a witness, since his silence keeps the ward's records in order
options.misconception: recasts a contrast as a practical job description

options.text: a foil, since his single concern measures the sister's scattered attention
a comfort, since the reader needs a quiet character in the long scenes
options.misconception: treats a foil as a device for reader rest

options.text: a rival, since the two men are presented as competing for the same post
options.misconception: turns a contrast into a contest for a position

questions.explanation: The porter's one narrow concern measures the sister's scattered attention, which is what a foil is for. A witness, a comfort and a rival are each a different kind of work.
questions.hint: Ask what his narrowness makes visible.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a thread contributes to a main action.
questions.stem: In a handover, the registrar asks why the story of a mislaid patient list is being followed at all, when the ward's main business is a waiting list that has run to nine hours.

options.text: Because the patient list explains why the waiting list grew so long
options.misconception: makes a subplot the explanation of the main plot's problem

options.text: Because the mislaid list gives the nursing staff something to talk about
options.misconception: treats a subplot as a topic for conversation

options.text: Because tracking it tells the ward who has been waiting and for how long
Because the list was mislaid by a character the reader will meet later
options.misconception: justifies a thread by a promised character, not its function

questions.explanation: The list thread functions by producing information the main business needs, namely who has waited and how long. Explaining the delay, providing talk and promising a character are not what it does.
questions.hint: Ask what the thread tells the ward.

questions.stem: A handover discusses a novel in which a long-running complaint about a missing blanket from the linen store runs beneath the ward's real business. What does the complaint thread do for the novel?

options.text: It establishes the habit of written complaints that a later discovery depends on
It measures the ward's ordinary scale before the crisis disturbs it
options.misconception: describes the thread's early function without its later use

options.text: It proves that the ward's linen arrangements were always inadequate
options.misconception: turns a prepared habit into a standing indictment

options.text: It shows how the family above the linen store spends its evenings
options.misconception: reads a domestic thread as a study of household habits

questions.explanation: The complaint earns its place by establishing the ward's ordinary scale and by planting a habit used later for a bigger discovery. Filler that informs nothing would not do this work.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of rotating who tells a story.
questions.stem: A handover records a reader who complained that the ward's history told in a series of handover notes is duller than a version told by one character. Explain what the handover makes of that complaint.

answer.exemplar: The handover makes of the complaint a case of mistaking the limits of one voice for the limits of the story. Handing the account to successive speakers lets the ward be known from several sides, and the resulting change of scale is what a reader experiences as the ward widening, so the dullness belongs to the complaint's assumption of a single holder rather than to the method itself.

questions.explanation: Handing the story to successive speakers gives the ward several sides, which is what a shifting point of view is for. Attention, scope and the superiority of one voice over another are other claims.
questions.hint: Ask what the changes of voice let a reader see.

options.misconception: turns a narrative device into a verification exercise

options.text: Because the change is made so the porter can be shown to have been lazy
options.misconception: assumes the second view exists to condemn the first

options.text: Because the change lets the reader compare two views of a single evening
Because the change is made so the reader hears the ward's routine from two angles
options.misconception: settles for a device that only adds variety

questions.explanation: When two people witness the same thing, moving the narration to the second sets up a comparison that can unsettle the first. Accuracy contests and variety are lesser readings.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret a narrator's ordering of facts as evidence of interest.

questions.stem: According to the note, what does the complaint about ordering show?

options.text: That she is a reliable narrator who orders facts sensibly for the reader
options.misconception: treats a consistent ordering as a mark of reliability

options.text: That she is a narrator whose ordering of facts carries an interest
That she is an unreliable narrator who has deliberately reversed the facts
options.misconception: jumps from ordering to deliberate falsification

options.text: That she is a narrator who cannot remember the order events happened in
options.misconception: explains a patterned ordering by memory lapse

questions.explanation: A consistent preference for good news first reveals an interest colouring the order of the telling, which is a claim about the narrator's stance. It does not by itself show falsity or faulty memory.

questions.learningObjective: Weigh a documented fault against a confident personal claim.

options.text: The note about rails is more reliable because records are always exact
options.misconception: assumes written records are automatically precise

options.text: The patient's account is more reliable because the patient was present
options.misconception: assumes presence guarantees an accurate account

options.text: Both accounts should be treated as equally true until someone admits fault
options.misconception: suspends judgement where the evidence is uneven

options.text: The note gives grounds for doubt, though not proof the patient is wrong

questions.explanation: The faulty-rails note is evidence to weigh against the patient's certainty, giving reason for doubt without settling the matter. Records are not automatically exact and presence guarantees nothing.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Determine what makes a brief character a foil.
questions.stem: A handover defends a minor character who appears in only three scenes by saying the author clearly meant her as a foil. What would have to be true for that defence to hold?

options.text: That her contrast with the other characters is what defines them
That she speaks in every scene in which the other character appears
options.misconception: sets a rule about joint appearances as the test

options.text: That her three scenes fall early enough to set up the ending
options.misconception: judges a foil by the position of its scenes in the plot

options.text: That the author stated in a preface that she was written as a foil
options.misconception: accepts an author's stated intention as proof of function

questions.explanation: A foil is defined by contrast, so the defence depends on what the contrast reveals rather than on the author's stated intention or the number of scenes. Briefness is no obstacle to the role.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a thread can work without shared characters.
questions.stem: A handover quotes a reader complaining that a thread about a school play is pointless because no character in it meets anyone in the main plot.

answer.exemplar: The complaint rests on a rule that is not the rule, because a thread can function without sharing characters if it changes what the main plot knows, fears or must decide. In this case the play draws the family into the school hall and forces the father to be seen by his neighbours, so what the reader learns about him comes entirely from a set of people who never enter the main plot at all.

questions.explanation: A thread can function without sharing characters if it changes what the main plot knows or fears, and the school play does that. Overlap, audience convenience and head counts are the wrong tests.
questions.hint: Ask what the play changes in the main plot.

questions.topic: A subplot's function in a novel
questions.learningObjective: Analyse how an early thread prepares a later crisis.
questions.stem: A handover sets out two novels for comparison. In the first, a thread about a child learning to swim opens early and closes with a drowning; in the second, a thread about a child learning to swim closes with the same drowning. The registrar asks what makes the first arrangement work.

options.text: The thread keeps the reader from suspecting a drowning before it happens
options.misconception: reads preparation as concealment of the ending

options.text: The thread gives the reader a second story while the main one is slow
options.misconception: credits a thread with keeping the reader busy

options.text: The thread establishes the confidence that the drowning then overturns
The thread explains to the reader why the child was near the water
options.misconception: treats the thread as supplying an explanation

questions.explanation: The thread prepares the confidence the drowning destroys, so it functions by setting up what the ending reverses. Concealment, distraction and explanation are all misreadings of the arrangement.
questions.hint: Ask what the thread sets up for the ending.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the effect of telling one incident in two vocabularies.

stimulus.body: A ward's story is told twice about the same incident, once in the language of the ward and once in the language of the family. The registrar asks what the doubling does for a reader who has been hearing only the ward's version.

questions.stem: According to the shift, what does the doubling mainly produce?

options.text: A version of events that is proven correct by being told twice
options.misconception: mistakes repetition for confirmation

options.text: A gap between accounts that the reader must interpret
Two separate stories that the reader must keep entirely apart
options.misconception: treats a doubled account as two unrelated narratives

options.text: A single account with the ward's wording quietly removed
options.misconception: reads the doubling as editing rather than juxtaposition

questions.explanation: Telling the same incident in two vocabularies opens a gap the reader must interpret, not a proof that one telling wins. Repetition is not confirmation, and the accounts are related.
questions.hint: Ask what sits between the two tellings.

options.misconception: treats a second account as a settled verdict

options.misconception: judges weight of evidence by the speaker's carelessness

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a narrator's marking of their own account.
questions.stem: A handover ends a section with the phrase, and this is only my account, before moving on to the next patient. What does that closing phrase tell a reader?

options.text: The speaker marks the telling as personal and open to dispute
The speaker admits the account may be false, so it should be discarded
options.misconception: mistakes a marked account for a withdrawn one

options.text: The speaker is being modest, so the account should be treated as certainly true
options.misconception: reads modesty as a guarantee of accuracy

options.text: The speaker warns that the next patient's file is also unreliable
options.misconception: takes the phrase to refer to a different case

questions.explanation: Calling the account only mine marks the telling as personal and contestable, which invites the reader to weigh it rather than accept or reject it outright. Modesty is not a guarantee of accuracy.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate praise without complaint as evidence.
questions.stem: A handover offers an account written by a patient who insists, over several pages, on how careful and untiring the staff were. Explain what a reader should make of that account.

answer.exemplar: A reader should treat the total absence of complaint as itself worth querying, because a long account from a patient in a hard week usually contains something, and here it contains only praise. That does not prove the praise false, but it does mean the account's reliability has to be established from detail rather than taken from the warmth of its tone, and the details in this case are conspicuously thin.

questions.explanation: A total absence of complaint in a long account is itself odd and worth examining. Exaggeration and motive are separate assumptions that do not follow from it.
questions.hint: Ask what is missing from the account.

Because the young supervisor is there to learn from her senior

options.misconception: turns a contrast into a contest for a position

questions.explanation: A foil works by contrast, so the older supervisor's cold precision measures the younger one's warmth and untidiness. Admiration, training and rivalry each misread the pairing.

options.misconception: credits a thread only for later information it carries

questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of delaying a rival account.
questions.stem: A handover describes a case where the account of the ward's worst night is given by the staff who worked it, and the account of the same night in a patient's letter is withheld until the end. Why does the delay matter?

It protects the staff from anything the patient's letter might say
options.misconception: reads a structural choice as protection for the staff

options.misconception: treats priority as proof of truth

options.text: It gives the reader time to forget the first account before the second arrives
options.misconception: assumes a delay exists to erase an earlier impression

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A viewpoint shift that supplies a reason
questions.learningObjective: Explain what pairing two tellings allows a reader to see.
questions.stem: A handover pairs two retellings of the same night, one from a ward sister and one from a patient, and asks what the pairing allows a reader to see that neither telling alone allows.

answer.exemplar: The pairing lets a reader see the selection each telling performs, because only side by side can the reader notice what the sister leaves out and what the patient adds. The device therefore comments on narration itself rather than adding a third fact about the night, and that is why neither account, read alone, could reveal the habits of its own speaker in the way the pair exposes them.

questions.explanation: Setting two tellings side by side exposes the selection and shaping each one performs, which neither account can show about itself. Reliability contests and merging all misread the device.
questions.hint: Ask what only the pairing can reveal.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A subplot's function in a novel
questions.learningObjective: Analyse why a constant thread may matter less than a short one.
questions.stem: A handover asks a group to say why a thread about a bus route, which appears in every chapter of a novel, does less for the book than a thread of three pages.

answer.exemplar: The bus thread does less because presence is not the same as pressure: appearing in every chapter tells the reader the novel has a thread, but it does not make the bus carry anything the crisis depends on. The three-page thread, by contrast, plants a habit or withholds a fact that the later crisis turns on, and a reader's sense of necessity comes from that turning rather than from sheer recurrence.

questions.explanation: Frequency is not function: a constant thread that does not press on the main action does less than a short one that changes what the story can do. The others praise content, not effect.
questions.hint: Ask whether the thread changes anything.

questions.learningObjective: Assess the reliability signalled by reported speech.
questions.stem: A handover quotes the sentence, I was told, of course, that the family had been informed. Why does the handover treat that sentence as revealing about the speaker?

options.text: It shows the speaker knows exactly what the family was told
options.misconception: reads a report of hearsay as direct knowledge

options.text: It shows the speaker is certain, since the report has been checked twice
options.misconception: reads of course as repeated verification

options.text: It shows the speaker is quoting the family in order to defend the ward
options.misconception: assumes a quoted report is always defensive

options.text: It shows the speaker is working from a report whose source is not identified

questions.explanation: The phrase I was told marks the speaker's information as second-hand, and of course adds a confident tone without naming a source. Confidence is not evidence of checking.
questions.hint: Ask where the speaker's information actually came from.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Assess reliability earned through corroborated detail.
questions.stem: A handover records that a patient's account of her last night on the ward is full of sensations, and that every one of them is confirmed by a fact in the file. What should a reader conclude?

options.text: Her impressions align with the record, so her account can be trusted where it offers no explanation
Her account is weak, since a patient has no way of knowing the ward's facts
options.misconception: judges a claim by the speaker's position, not the evidence

options.text: Her account is unreliable, since a file will confirm whatever it is asked to confirm
options.misconception: assumes every document in a case file is reliable

options.text: Nothing follows, because the file and the patient are both interested parties
options.misconception: dismisses a document as interested in every case

questions.explanation: Sensations repeatedly confirmed by the file show the speaker's impressions aligning with the record, which supports trusting her. Reliability here is earned in detail, claim by claim.
questions.hint: Ask whether the file supports each impression.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a pair of contrasted characters works.
questions.stem: A handover remarks that the young porter is loud, ambitious and untidy, and that the senior porter is quiet, cautious and neat. Explain what that pairing sets up in the story.

answer.exemplar: The pairing sets up a measurement of the younger porter by the older one, since a foil exists to make a quality legible by contrast and here the senior man's caution and neatness give the younger man's loudness and untidiness a scale. The reader is meant to judge the younger man against the standard the ward holds itself to, which is a different effect from a rivalry or a promotion story.

questions.explanation: The senior porter's qualities are defined against the younger man's, so the pairing shows one character measuring another. Jealousy and promotion decisions are not what it establishes.
questions.hint: Ask who is defined by whom.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the function of a domestic thread.
questions.stem: The registrar hears about a patient whose family brings in a second blanket every night and takes the first away again in the morning. The registrar asks whether this family business belongs in the account of a ward where a discharge has gone wrong.

options.text: A subplot that distracts from the discharge, which is what the ward cares about
options.misconception: judges a thread by whether it keeps the focus narrow

options.text: A subplot that proves the family cannot be trusted with the patient
options.misconception: reads a thread as evidence against a family

options.text: A subplot that shapes the household's silence about the discharge
A subplot that has no function at all, since nobody mentions it again
options.misconception: tests a thread by whether it is named at the end

questions.explanation: The thread belongs because the repeated blanket explains the household's silence about the discharge, which presses on the main action. Distraction, distrust and final mention are the wrong tests.
questions.hint: Ask what the blanket explains.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A subplot's function in a novel
questions.learningObjective: Analyse why an early thread can be necessary.

stimulus.body: A handover compares two novels in which a separate thread is opened early, and asks why one of them feels necessary while the other feels like an errand. The registrar notes that in the first novel the thread establishes a habit of leaving a door unlocked, and the later crisis depends on that habit.

questions.stem: According to the shift, why does the first novel's early thread feel necessary?

options.text: Because it is told with more skill and better phrasing
options.misconception: credits quality of writing rather than structural necessity

options.text: Because it shows the habit that the later crisis will exploit
Because it is longer, so the reader is prepared for it
options.misconception: uses length of thread as evidence of its function

options.text: Because it is shorter, so the reader is not bored
options.misconception: treats brevity as the marker of a purposeful thread

questions.explanation: A thread earns its early place by establishing something the crisis later exploits, which is why one chapter feels necessary. Skill, length and brevity describe manner rather than function.
questions.hint: Ask what the thread does before the crisis arrives.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the effect of relaying a finding through a third party.
questions.stem: During the handover, the registrar describes a case where the ward's findings were relayed to the family by a nurse who had never met the patient. Why does the handover treat the relay as a point-of-view decision?

options.text: It makes the ward's findings more reliable, being doubly checked
options.misconception: assumes relay always improves accuracy

options.text: It hides the ward's judgement behind the messenger's neutral words
options.misconception: jumps to a claim of deliberate concealment

options.text: It confirms the family should have been present at the ward round
options.misconception: turns a narrative choice into a procedural complaint

options.text: It narrows what the family can know to what the relay carried

questions.explanation: Any relay restricts the account to what the relay carried, and that restriction is the point-of-view effect worth naming. Relay does not add checking, and it does not by itself prove concealment.
questions.hint: Ask what the family can know after the relay.
